title.en: State and society in the Indian subcontinent up to 1000 CE
Kings, dharma and the idea of one land

text.en: More than a thousand years ago, rulers across the subcontinent governed in many different ways. Yet ideas such as dharma and the chakravarti samrat helped people see the land as one cultural whole.

Early states in the subcontinent grew from janapadas into larger mahajanapadas, with kings, taxes and armies.
The Mauryan empire under Chandragupta and Ashoka brought much of the subcontinent under one rule.
Ashoka's edicts spread the idea of dhamma, which stressed non-violence, tolerance and care for people.
The Gupta period is remembered for advances in mathematics, astronomy, literature and art.
Dharma meant duty and right conduct, and kings were expected to rule by dharma.
A chakravarti samrat was a ruler who aimed to unite regions under one wide authority, promoting a shared political idea.
Society was organised in villages, guilds and learning centres like Nalanda; trade linked the subcontinent with other lands.
Southern kingdoms like the Cholas and Pallavas built strong states, temples and sea trade.

problem.en: Why are Ashoka's edicts important sources?

text.en: They were carved on rocks and pillars in public places.
They tell us about his policies and values.
They are found across the subcontinent.

prompt.en: How did dharma and the idea of the chakravarti help unity?

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the subcontinent had one ruler throughout

points.en: Mauryas and Guptas built large states.
